title: Impact of Local Labor Demand Shocks on Wages

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Two-Stage Least Squares (IV) using a Bartik shift–share instrument.  
• Why IV? The observed local labor-demand variable x may be endogenous (simultaneously determined with wages or affected by omitted local shocks). The Bartik instrument z exploits national industry growth rates—plausibly exogenous to any one region—scaled by pre-determined regional industry shares, delivering exogenous variation in local labor demand.  
• Key assumptions  
 1. Relevance: Cov(z, x) ≠ 0 – national industry shocks move local labor demand.  
 2. Exclusion / exogeneity: E[z · u] = 0 – conditional on controls, the Bartik shift affects wages only through its impact on local labor demand, not via other channels.  

## 2. R Code
```r
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# Impact of Local Labor Demand Shocks on Wages – IV analysis
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# Load packages
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(readr)     # Read CSV
  library(AER)       # ivreg
  library(lmtest)    # coeftest
  library(sandwich)  # robust vcov
  library(dplyr)     # data wrangling
})

# 1. Read data
data_path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s83_data.csv"
df <- read_csv(data_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

# Ensure correct types
df <- df %>%
  mutate(z = as.numeric(z))  # ivreg expects numeric

# 2. Baseline OLS (naïve)
ols <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = df)
ols_robust <- coeftest(ols, vcov = vcovHC(ols, type = "HC1"))

# 3. IV: 2SLS with Bartik instrument
iv <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df)
iv_robust <- coeftest(iv, vcov = vcovHC(iv, type = "HC1"))

# 4. First-stage diagnostics
first_stage <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = df)
fs_robust <- coeftest(first_stage, vcov = vcovHC(first_stage, type = "HC1"))
fs_Fstat <- waldtest(first_stage, . ~ controls, vcov = vcovHC(first_stage, type = "HC1"))$F[2]

# 5. Reduced form (y on instrument)
rf <- lm(y ~ z + controls, data = df)
rf_robust <- coeftest(rf, vcov = vcovHC(rf, type = "HC1"))

# 6. Simple robustness check: add quadratic control
iv_quad <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls + I(controls^2) | z + controls + I(controls^2), data = df)
iv_quad_robust <- coeftest(iv_quad, vcov = vcovHC(iv_quad, type = "HC1"))

# 7. Print concise results
cat("\n========== Baseline OLS (robust SE) ==========\n")
print(ols_robust["x", ])

cat("\n========== First Stage (robust SE) ==========\n")
print(fs_robust["z", ])
cat(sprintf("First-stage F-statistic on instrument: %.2f\n", fs_Fstat))

cat("\n========== 2SLS / IV (robust SE) ==========\n")
print(iv_robust["x", ])

cat("\n========== Reduced Form (robust SE) ==========\n")
print(rf_robust["z", ])

cat("\n========== IV with Quadratic Control (robust SE) ==========\n")
print(iv_quad_robust["x", ])
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Economic intuition and prior literature (e.g., Bartik 1991; Notowidigdo 2020) suggest that positive labor-demand shocks raise local wages. We therefore expect:  
• Sign: positive.  
• Magnitude: a one-standard-deviation increase in local labor demand (x) is likely to raise wages (y) by roughly 0.4–0.8 standard deviations—i.e., an IV coefficient in the 0.4 – 0.8 range.  
We also anticipate a strong first-stage F-stat (>10), confirming instrument relevance, and that robustness checks (quadratic controls) leave the estimate broadly unchanged.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use Bartik shift-share as an instrument for local labor demand.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The analysis reveals a significant positive effect of local labor demand on wages.
